lessons.title: How a page loads: HTML, subresources, JavaScript and the DOM

blocks.md:
Every rule in this course is about one question: **when code from one place runs in your browser, what is it allowed to touch?** To answer it you first need to know what a web page is made of. When you type `https://shop.example.com` the browser sends one HTTP GET request (you met requests, responses and headers in the networking course) and gets back one document written in **HTML** (HyperText Markup Language). *Hypertext* is text containing links to other text; in 1989 and 1990 Tim Berners-Lee, a computer scientist at CERN (the European particle physics laboratory), proposed the Web with hypertext as its basis. *Markup* means the content is wrapped in tags such as `

...

` that describe its structure.

blocks.code: Hello
blocks.caption: A tiny page served by https://shop.example.com. Three of its lines point at other files, two of them on other servers.

blocks.md: A tag with its content is an **element**. Some elements point at other files the page needs, called **subresources**: the stylesheet in ``, the scripts in `

blocks.title: One page, four requests to three servers

scenes.caption: The navigation: one GET for the page itself. The response body is the HTML above.
Parsing reaches the stylesheet link and asks the same server for it.
The script tag points at a different server. Parsing pauses until lib.js arrives and has run.
The image comes from a third server. The page now depends on three operators, and the shop controls only one of them.

blocks.md:
**JavaScript** (JS) is the programming language browsers run inside pages. Brendan Eich, a programmer at Netscape (the company behind the Netscape Navigator browser), created it in 1995. It first shipped in a Navigator 2.0 beta in September 1995 under the name LiveScript, and was renamed JavaScript for the release that December. Despite the name it is a different language from Java.

Scripts do not edit the HTML text. The browser turns the parsed HTML into the **DOM** (Document Object Model): the page as a tree of objects, one per element, that scripts can read and change. *Document* because it models the page, *object model* because each part is an object with properties and methods. Change the DOM and the screen changes.

blocks.title: What the inline script does to the DOM

scenes.caption: getElementById finds the h1 element in the DOM tree. h is now a reference to that object, not a copy of the text.
Reading a property of the DOM object gives the current text.
Assigning the property changes the tree, and the browser repaints the heading. No request to the server happened.
document.cookie returns the cookies the page may see as one string (cookies are lesson 4).
fetch() asks the browser to send an HTTP request from script. The browser attaches cookies for shop.example.com and hands the response back.

blocks.md: A script runs with the authority of **the page that includes it**, not the server it came from. `lib.js` from `cdn.example.net` runs as if `shop.example.com` had written it: it can read and change the shop's DOM, read the shop's visible cookies and send requests to the shop with the user's cookies. Including a script is handing over your keys.

That one fact explains most of web security. Pages mix content from many origins, and the browser needs rules for who may read what. The rest of the course builds them up: **origins** name the owner of each piece (lesson 2), the **same-origin policy** keeps owners apart (lesson 3), and cookies, CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing), CSP (Content Security Policy), framing rules, HTTPS (encrypted HTTP) and process isolation each tighten or loosen that wall; each gets its own lesson.

blocks.prompt: A month later the company running cdn.example.net is compromised and lib.js is replaced. The shop's own server is untouched. What can the new lib.js do on shop pages?
blocks.reveal: Everything the shop's own code can do: read what the user types into the shop's forms, rewrite prices, and send requests to the shop with the user's cookies attached. The browser has no idea the file changed, because it runs whatever arrives at that URL. This is exactly how the polyfill.io takeover in 2024 reached more than 100,000 sites, and lesson 12 shows the defences (Subresource Integrity, self-hosting, CSP).

blocks.question: A page has, in order: `
options: a.js, because a plain script tag blocks parsing
Only b.png, because images are large
c.js, because async means the parser waits for it
None of them; browsers never pause parsing
blocks.explain: A script tag without async or defer stops the parser until the script is fetched and executed. Images are fetched in parallel, and async scripts run whenever they arrive without blocking the parser.

blocks.question: Why can a script loaded from a third-party CDN (content delivery network, a company that serves files for other sites) read the cookies of the page that includes it (unless they are marked HttpOnly, a flag that hides them from scripts)?
options: Because CDNs are trusted by browsers by default
Because the CDN also sets the cookies
Because an included script runs in the including page's context, with that page's origin
It cannot; scripts can only read cookies of the server they came from
blocks.explain: The browser judges a script by the page it runs in, not by where its bytes came from. An included script is part of the page, so it gets the page's DOM, its non-HttpOnly cookies via document.cookie, and the ability to send requests as the page.

lessons.title: Origins and sites: how the browser names who owns a page

blocks.md:
The browser needs a name for "who owns this page", so it can keep different owners apart. That name is the **origin**: the combination of **scheme** (the protocol, `http` or `https`), **host** (the domain name or IP address) and **port** (the TCP port, 80 by default for http and 443 for https). MDN Web Docs (Mozilla's reference site for web developers, used as a main source in this course) calls it the scheme/host/port *tuple*, a tuple being an ordered group of values that together form one thing.

Two URLs are **same-origin** only if all three parts match exactly. The path, query string and fragment do not matter.

blocks.title: Comparing a URL with the page's origin

scenes.caption: Only the path differs. Scheme, host and port all match, so the two URLs are same-origin and same-site.
http instead of https. The scheme differs (and so does the default port), so it is cross-origin. Since 2019 a site includes the scheme too, so it is also cross-site.
An explicit port 8443. Ports differ, so it is cross-origin. A site ignores ports, so it is still same-site.
A sibling subdomain. Hosts differ, so cross-origin. Both share the registrable domain example.com, so same-site.
A look-alike host. It starts with shop.example.com but its registrable domain is evil.net: cross-origin and cross-site. String prefix checks get this wrong (lesson 7).

blocks.caption: Paste these into a browser console. An origin is serialized as scheme://host, plus :port only when the port is not the default.

blocks.md:
Some rules use a coarser unit, the **site**. A site is the scheme plus the **registrable domain**: the public suffix plus one more label. A **public suffix** is a name under which anyone can register their own domain, such as `com`, `co.uk` or `github.io`. These are also called eTLDs (effective top-level domains) because they behave like a TLD (top-level domain, the last label such as `com`), and the registrable domain is called eTLD+1.

You cannot work this out from the name alone, so browsers use the [Public Suffix List](https://publicsuffix.org/), a list started by Mozilla and maintained as a community resource. Under it, `alice.github.io` and `bob.github.io` are **different sites**, because `github.io` is a public suffix, while `www.example.com` and `login.example.com` are the **same site**, `https://example.com`.

Same-site is not same-origin. `login.example.com` and `blog.example.com` are same-site but cross-origin. A weak subdomain (an old blog, a marketing page run by a vendor) is "same-site" with your login page, and cookie rules and SameSite (lesson 5) treat it as a friend.

Which unit applies where:

- **Origin**: the same-origin policy, CORS, `postMessage` checks, storage such as `localStorage` (a key-value store a page can keep in the browser), CSP's `'self'` keyword.
- **Site**: the `SameSite` cookie attribute and Chrome's Site Isolation (lesson 13).
- **Domain (no scheme or port)**: cookie scoping with `Domain` and HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security, lesson 11), which identifies a host by name only.

Keeping these three straight answers many "why did the browser allow that?" questions later.

blocks.question: Is `https://app.example.com:8443` same-origin with `https://app.example.com`, and is it same-site?
options: Same-origin and same-site
Cross-origin but same-site
Cross-origin and cross-site
Same-origin but cross-site
blocks.explain: The ports differ (8443 vs the default 443), so the origins differ. A site is the scheme plus registrable domain and ignores ports, so both are the site https://example.com.

blocks.question: Why are `alice.github.io` and `bob.github.io` cross-site, while `www.example.com` and `login.example.com` are same-site?
options: GitHub sends a special header that splits sites
Any domain with more than two labels is always cross-site
Because their IP addresses differ
github.io is on the Public Suffix List, so each user's subdomain is its own registrable domain
blocks.explain: The Public Suffix List marks github.io as a suffix under which anyone can register a name, so the registrable domains are alice.github.io and bob.github.io. example.com is not a public suffix, so both of its subdomains share the registrable domain example.com.

blocks.prompt: Before late 2019, `http://www.example.com` and `https://www.example.com` counted as the same site. What changed, and why does it matter?
blocks.reveal: The definition of site now includes the scheme ("schemeful same-site"). An http page and an https page of the same domain are therefore cross-site. That matters because anyone on the network can tamper with plain http traffic: if the http version counted as same-site, an attacker who injects content into it would get the trust that SameSite cookies give to same-site requests.

lessons.title: The same-origin policy: what it blocks and what it lets through

blocks.md:
You are logged in to your webmail in one tab. In another tab you open a page from `evil.example`. Its JavaScript calls `fetch("https://mail.example/inbox")`. If the browser handed the response to that script, any page you visit could read your email.

The **same-origin policy** (SOP) is the browser rule that stops this: a document or script from one origin has only very limited access to resources and documents from another origin. It does not stop everything that crosses origins, and the exceptions are where most web attacks live.

MDN sorts cross-origin interactions into three kinds: 1. **Writes are typically allowed.** Links, redirects and form submissions to other origins go through. The other server receives the request and may act on it. 2. **Embedding is typically allowed.** `

blocks.title: The policy blocks reading, not sending

scenes.caption: Script on evil.example asks the browser to fetch the victim's inbox from another origin.
The request really is sent, with an Origin header naming the caller. By default a cross-origin fetch carries no cookies, but the server still sees the request.
The server answers. The response contains no CORS header granting evil.example access.
The browser withholds the body. The script gets a TypeError and the console logs a CORS error. This is the read that SOP blocks.
Now the page submits a hidden HTML form to mail.example. Forms are cross-origin writes, which SOP allows. Whether cookies ride along depends on SameSite (lesson 5).

If the server trusts the cookie alone, the change goes through. SOP never promised to stop this; it is cross-site request forgery (CSRF: another site forges a request your browser sends), covered in the next courses.

blocks.caption: The script is told only that something failed. For security the details of a CORS failure go to the developer console, not to JavaScript.

blocks.md: The same-origin policy limits what a page can **read** from other origins. It does not stop a page from **sending** requests to them, and it does nothing at all to code that is already running inside your origin. State-changing endpoints need their own protection on the server.

The same split applies to windows. A page can hold references to other windows, such as an iframe's `contentWindow` or a popup from `window.open()`. Across origins only a few things work through those references: `postMessage()` (lesson 10), `close()`, `focus()`, reading `closed` and `length`, and writing `location` to navigate the window. Almost everything else, including its DOM, throws an error (a few navigation properties such as `parent`, `top` and `opener` can also be read).

Browser storage is also split by origin: each origin gets its own `localStorage` and IndexedDB. Cookies are the exception and follow older, looser domain rules, which is why they get two lessons of their own.

Older pages set `document.domain` to a parent domain to relax the check. MDN marks this deprecated because it undermines the policy, and since Chrome 115 the setter has no effect unless the page sends an `Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?0` header.

**Real case: the Samy worm (October 2005).** Samy Kamkar, then a 19-year-old developer, found a way to put script into a profile on MySpace, the largest social network of the time,, and that script added the viewer as a friend and copied itself into the viewer's profile. Kamkar's own write-up shows SOP at work: profiles were shown on `profile.myspace.com`, but the add-friend request had to go to `www.myspace.com`, a different host and so a different origin, and the script's request there was refused. The worm's answer was to reload the page on `www.myspace.com`, after which every request was same-origin. It then simply read the page that contained MySpace's random anti-forgery token and used it.

Within 20 hours of its release on 4 October 2005, over a million users had run it. The lesson: SOP protects origins from **each other**. Script injected *into* an origin, called cross-site scripting or XSS (X for "cross", because CSS already meant Cascading Style Sheets), gets all of that origin's power. XSS is the subject of the client-side attacks course.

**Defender view.** You do not need to switch SOP on, and you cannot switch it off for your users. Your jobs are to avoid weakening it (careless CORS headers, `document.domain`, `postMessage` listeners that trust anyone), to protect cross-origin writes on the server with SameSite cookies and anti-forgery tokens, and to keep attacker script out of your origin. Server logs are useful here: requests to state-changing endpoints whose `Origin` header names a site you do not own are a signal worth alerting on.

blocks.question: A page on evil.example contains `` and runs `fetch("https://bank.example/balance")`. With no CORS headers from bank.example, what happens?
options: The image displays; the fetch request is sent but the script cannot read the balance
Both are blocked; nothing is sent to bank.example
The image is blocked but the fetch succeeds
Both succeed, because GET requests are always readable
blocks.explain: Embedding an image is allowed cross-origin, so the logo shows. The fetch is sent too (SOP does not stop sending), but without an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header naming evil.example the browser withholds the response body from the script.

blocks.question: Which statement about the same-origin policy is true?
options: It prevents other sites from sending POST requests to your server
It stops script injected into your own pages from reading your cookies
It keeps localStorage separate per origin
It applies only to https pages
blocks.explain: Storage such as localStorage and IndexedDB is partitioned by origin. SOP does not stop cross-origin writes such as form POSTs, does nothing against script running inside your origin (XSS), and applies to http and https alike.

lessons.title: Cookies, sessions, and how Firesheep hijacked them in 2010

blocks.md:
HTTP is stateless: each request stands alone, so the server needs a way to recognise you on the next click. The answer is the **cookie** (named after the Unix programmers' "magic cookie", a token a program receives and hands back unchanged): a small `name=value` pair the server asks the browser to store, using the `Set-Cookie` response header. The browser sends it back on later requests to that server in the `Cookie` request header, automatically, without any script asking.

Most sites store a **session identifier** in that cookie: a long random value that is the key to a record on the server ("this session belongs to Ana, logged in at 09:14"). RFC 6265bis (RFC means Request for Comments, the IETF's numbered document series; "bis" marks a revision), the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) draft that defines cookies, recommends exactly this pattern, because the cookie then reveals nothing by itself.

blocks.code:
POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: social.example
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

user=ana&password=correct-horse

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: /home
Set-Cookie: sid=7f3a9c41e2b8; Path=/

GET /home HTTP/1.1
Host: social.example
Cookie: sid=7f3a9c41e2b8
blocks.caption: Log in once, then every later request carries the session cookie. The server looks up sid in its session store to know who you are.

blocks.md: A session cookie is a **bearer token**: whoever bears (holds) it is, as far as the server is concerned, the logged-in user. No password is needed to use it. Protecting the session ID matters as much as protecting the password, for as long as the session is valid.

**Real case: Firesheep (October 2010).** On 24 October 2010, at the ToorCon 12 security conference, software developer Eric Butler released Firesheep, a Firefox extension. Butler's announcement explains the gap it exposed: sites commonly encrypted the login form, so the password was safe, but then served every later page over plain HTTP, so the session cookie crossed the network unencrypted on each request.

On an open Wi-Fi network anyone nearby can capture that traffic. Firesheep did it with one button: it listened, showed the name and photo of each person it saw using a supported site, and a double-click logged you in as them. The EFF (Electronic Frontier Foundation) listed Facebook, Twitter, Yelp and Flickr among the affected sites. Butler called the attack HTTP session hijacking, also known as sidejacking.

blocks.title: Firesheep: an encrypted login, then a cookie sent in clear

scenes.caption: Ana logs in over HTTPS. The password is encrypted, and the session cookie comes back encrypted too.
The site then redirects to plain HTTP pages. Every request now carries Cookie: sid=7f3a in clear text over the shared Wi-Fi.
The same radio frames reach every device on the network. Firesheep on the nearby laptop reads the Cookie header.
The laptop replays the cookie. The server cannot tell the two browsers apart and answers as if it were Ana.
The fix: every page over HTTPS and the cookie marked Secure, so it is never sent over HTTP. The overheard frames are ciphertext.

blocks.md:
Butler's conclusion was blunt: the only effective fix is full end-to-end encryption, meaning HTTPS (HTTP over TLS, Transport Layer Security) on every page, not just the login. The EFF used the moment to push sitewide HTTPS, quoting Google's report that turning on HTTPS for all Gmail users needed no extra machines and that TLS accounted for less than 1% of CPU load on its front ends.

Two more pieces close the gap completely, and both come later in this course: the `Secure` cookie attribute, which keeps a cookie off plain HTTP even if some page or an attacker's injected link uses `http://` (lesson 5), and HSTS, which makes the browser refuse plain HTTP for the whole site (lesson 11).

blocks.code:
# Vulnerable (2010 pattern): HTTPS only for the login form
Set-Cookie: sid=7f3a9c41e2b8; Path=/
# ...later pages served over http://social.example/

# Fixed: HTTPS everywhere, cookie never sent over HTTP,
# hidden from page scripts, browser told to refuse HTTP
Set-Cookie: __Host-sid=7f3a9c41e2b8; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Path=/
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains
blocks.caption: Each attribute in the fixed line is explained in the next lesson, HSTS in lesson 11.

blocks.md: **Defender view.** *Prevent*: HTTPS on every page, `Secure` on every session cookie, HSTS; issue a fresh session ID at login so an ID planted before login is useless. *Detect*: one session ID used from two IP addresses or two different user agents at the same time, or jumping between distant locations, is the classic hijack signal in authentication and web server logs. *Respond*: revoke the session on the server (deleting the record makes the stolen cookie worthless), then force re-login. RFC 6265bis also warns that encrypting or signing the cookie's contents does not help here, because an attacker can still transplant the whole cookie to another browser and replay it.

blocks.question: Why did Firesheep work against sites that already used HTTPS for their login page?
options: Their HTTPS certificates were invalid
The session cookie was sent over plain HTTP on the pages after login
Firesheep could decrypt HTTPS traffic on open Wi-Fi
The passwords were stored without hashing
blocks.explain: Only the login was encrypted. Every later request went over plain HTTP with the session cookie in the Cookie header, and on a shared network anyone could read and replay it. Firesheep never needed the password or any decryption.

blocks.question: A developer proposes encrypting the session cookie's value with a server key as the fix for sidejacking. Why is that not enough?
options: Encryption makes the cookie too long for browsers
Browsers reject encrypted cookies
It is enough; an encrypted cookie cannot be used by anyone else
The attacker can still copy the whole encrypted cookie and replay it; the server will accept it
blocks.explain: The server only checks that the cookie it receives is valid. A stolen encrypted cookie is still valid. The fix is to keep the cookie off the network in clear text (HTTPS everywhere plus Secure) and to revoke sessions on suspicion.

lessons.title: Cookie attributes: Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, Domain, Path, prefixes

blocks.md:
A bare `Set-Cookie: sid=abc` is sent to the setting host on every request, over HTTP or HTTPS, and is readable by any script on the page. Attributes, added after semicolons, narrow that down. Each one answers a different question:

- **Secure**: only send over HTTPS (localhost is exempt). Pages served over `http:` cannot set it.
- **HttpOnly**: hide the cookie from JavaScript (`document.cookie`). It is still sent with requests, including those made by `fetch()`.
- **SameSite**: whether to send it on requests that come from another site.
- **Domain** and **Path**: which hosts and URL paths receive it.
- **Expires** or **Max-Age**: when it dies. Without either it is a *session cookie* in the browser's sense (one that lasts only for the browser session, not to be confused with a cookie holding a session ID), deleted when the browser closes (though session restore can keep it alive).

blocks.code:
# Weak: readable by any script, sent over HTTP, sent cross-site in
# browsers without Chrome-style default Lax,
# shared with every subdomain, lives for a year
Set-Cookie: sid=7f3a9c41e2b8; Domain=example.com; Max-Age=31536000

# Strong: host-only, HTTPS-only, invisible to scripts,
# not sent on cross-site subrequests, ends with the browser session
Set-Cookie: __Host-sid=7f3a9c41e2b8; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Path=/
blocks.caption: Max-Age is in seconds: 31536000 is 365 days. The strong version has no Max-Age, so it is a session cookie.

blocks.md:
**Domain and Path.** Without `Domain`, a cookie is *host-only*: sent only to the exact host that set it. With `Domain=example.com`, it goes to `example.com` and **every** subdomain. A host can only name itself or a parent domain, never a public suffix such as `com` or `co.uk`; the browser ignores cookies that break this. `Path=/docs` limits sending to URLs under `/docs`, but MDN and RFC 6265bis both warn that Path is not a security boundary: a page on another path of the same origin can still reach the cookie through script.

RFC 6265bis spells out two more weaknesses. Cookies are not isolated by port: a service on port 8080 sees the cookies of the service on port 443 of the same host. And they have **weak integrity**: `foo.example.com` can set a cookie with `Domain=example.com` that `bar.example.com` will receive and cannot tell apart from its own.

**SameSite** uses the *site* from lesson 2.

- `Strict`: sent only when the request comes from the same site. Even following a link from another site to yours arrives without it.
- `Lax`: also sent on cross-site requests that are a **top-level navigation** (the address bar changes) **and** use a safe method such as GET. Not sent on cross-site `fetch()`, images, scripts, iframe loads or form POSTs.
- `None`: sent on every request, but only accepted together with `Secure`.

Chrome treats a cookie with no SameSite attribute as Lax (since Chrome 80), with one temporary relaxation: such a default-Lax cookie is still sent on a cross-site top-level POST if it was set within the last two minutes. Other browsers differ, so set the attribute explicitly.

blocks.title: Is the cookie sent? (1 = yes, 0 = no)

scenes.caption: Every mode sends the cookie on requests from your own site. The differences are all about requests started by other sites.
A user clicks a link on another site to yours. Lax sends the cookie, so they arrive logged in. Strict does not.

A hidden form on an attacker's site POSTs to yours. Only None sends the cookie. This is why SameSite is a strong CSRF defence. (Chrome's default-Lax still sends it within two minutes of the cookie being set.)
Subresources, script fetches and framed pages started by another site get the cookie only under None. Framed pages therefore look logged out, which also blunts clickjacking (lesson 9).
None is for cookies that must work when embedded elsewhere (widgets, cross-site sign-in). Even then, browser and user settings that block third-party cookies may drop them.

blocks.md:
**Cookie prefixes** turn the weak-integrity problem around. The browser enforces rules based on the cookie's *name*:

- `__Secure-` names are accepted only with `Secure`, from an HTTPS page.
- `__Host-` names additionally must have `Path=/` and **no** `Domain`. So a `__Host-` cookie is locked to the exact host that set it, and a sibling subdomain cannot plant or overwrite it.

A browser that does not understand prefixes accepts the cookie anyway, so prefixes are a hardening step on top of correct attributes, not a replacement.

blocks.caption: HttpOnly stops an injected script from stealing the cookie value, but not from sending requests with it.

blocks.md: HttpOnly is often oversold. It stops cookie **theft** by script, so an attacker cannot carry the session to their own machine. It does not stop script running in your page from **using** the session right there, which is what the Samy worm did. XSS still needs to be prevented at its source.

**Defender view.** Audit every `Set-Cookie` your applications send (browser developer tools list each cookie with its attributes). Session and auth cookies should be `__Host-` prefixed, `Secure`, `HttpOnly` and `SameSite=Lax` or `Strict`. A `Domain=` attribute on a session cookie means every subdomain, including the forgotten ones, receives it; treat that as a finding.

blocks.question: Which of these Set-Cookie headers, sent by https://shop.example.com, will a supporting browser reject?
options: `__Host-sid=1; Secure; Path=/; Domain=example.com`
`__Secure-sid=1; Secure; Domain=example.com`
`__Host-sid=1; Secure; Path=/`
`sid=1; Secure; HttpOnly`
blocks.explain: A __Host- cookie must have Secure, Path=/ and no Domain attribute. The first one sets Domain, so it is rejected. __Secure- only requires Secure from an HTTPS page, so Domain is allowed there.

blocks.question: A session cookie is set with `SameSite=Lax; Secure; HttpOnly`. An attacker's page auto-submits a hidden form that POSTs to your /transfer endpoint. Does the cookie go with it?
options: Yes, because form submissions are top-level navigations
Yes, because HttpOnly cookies are always sent
No: Lax only sends on cross-site top-level navigations with a safe method, and POST is not safe
No, because Secure blocks all cross-site requests
blocks.explain: Lax requires both a top-level navigation and a safe method like GET. A cross-site POST fails the second test, so an explicitly Lax cookie is left off. (Chrome's default-Lax for cookies without the attribute has a two-minute exception, another reason to set it explicitly.)

lessons.title: CORS: how a server opts in to cross-origin reads

blocks.md:
SOP blocks cross-origin reads, but real applications need some. The front end at `https://app.example.com` must read JSON from `https://api.example.com`, a different origin. **CORS** (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is the opt-in: the server adds response headers saying which other origins may read the response, and the browser enforces them.

The WHATWG Fetch standard (the specification that defines how browsers fetch anything, written by the Web Hypertext Application Technology Working Group) explains why it must be opt-in: otherwise pages could read responses from servers behind a firewall, such as company intranets, and responses fetched with the user's cookies.

blocks.code:
GET /items HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Origin: https://app.example.com

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com
Vary: Origin

[{"id": 7, "name": "lamp"}]
blocks.caption: The browser adds Origin. The server's Access-Control-Allow-Origin (ACAO) must equal that origin exactly, or be *, for the script to see the body.

blocks.md:
`Access-Control-Allow-Origin` takes exactly one value: a single origin, `null`, or `*` (any origin, allowed only for requests without credentials). It cannot hold a list. A server that trusts several origins must check the request's `Origin` against its own list and echo back the one that matched.

Important: in this exchange the request reached the server and the server did its work **before** the browser checked the header. For simple reads that is harmless. For requests that could change data, the browser asks first.

**Simple requests** need no advance check. MDN's term comes from the old CORS spec: a request is simple if it uses GET, HEAD or POST, sets only a few safelisted headers (`Accept`, `Accept-Language`, `Content-Language`, `Content-Type`, and a single-range `Range`), and any `Content-Type` is one of `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, `multipart/form-data` or `text/plain`. The reasoning: an HTML `<form>` could always send exactly these requests to any origin, so servers already had to cope with them.

Anything else, such as PUT or DELETE, a JSON body, or a header outside the safelist such as `Authorization`, triggers a **preflight**: an automatic `OPTIONS` request (OPTIONS is the HTTP method for asking what a resource supports) sent first. The real request is sent only if the server's answer allows it.

blocks.title: A simple request, a preflighted one, and a refused one

scenes.caption: A plain GET is simple: the browser sends it immediately with an Origin header.
The response names app.example in ACAO, so the browser releases the body to the script.
A PUT with a JSON body is not simple. Before sending it, the browser sends OPTIONS with Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT and Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type.
The server answers 204 with Allow-Methods: PUT, Allow-Headers: Content-Type and ACAO: app. Only now is the real PUT sent.
A DELETE the server does not list. The preflight answer does not allow it, so the browser never sends the DELETE at all and the script gets a TypeError.

blocks.caption: The browser decides simple versus preflighted from the method, headers and content type; the page cannot skip the preflight.

blocks.md:
The preflight answer can be cached. `Access-Control-Max-Age: 86400` lets the browser reuse it for up to 86,400 seconds (24 hours), though each browser caps the value; without the header the default is 5 seconds. Preflight requests never carry cookies.

When a response depends on the `Origin` header, the server must also send `Vary: Origin`. The Fetch standard requires this so that a shared cache does not store the answer for one origin and replay it to another.

CORS is enforced by **browsers**, about **reading**. It is not access control on your server. `curl` or a script outside a browser ignores it completely, and a simple request reaches your server even when the browser will later hide the response. Authentication and authorization still have to happen on the server for every request.

blocks.prompt: A page on https://app.example.com calls `fetch` with method POST and header `Content-Type: application/json` to https://api.example.com. Will the browser send a preflight?
blocks.reveal: Yes. POST is a safelisted method, but `application/json` is not one of the three safelisted content types, so the request is not simple. The browser sends `OPTIONS` with `Access-Control-Request-Method: POST` and `Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type`, and sends the POST only if the reply allows both. Many JSON APIs rely on this as a side benefit: an attacker's page cannot send them a cross-origin `application/json` POST without the server's permission. That only helps if the server rejects bodies sent with other content types, because a `text/plain` POST holding JSON is still a simple request.

blocks.question: A preflight response includes `Access-Control-Max-Age: 600`. What does that do?
options: The real response may be cached by the browser for 600 seconds
The browser may reuse this preflight's answer for up to 600 seconds instead of sending a new OPTIONS request
The server will reject requests older than 600 seconds
The cookie set by the response expires after 600 seconds
blocks.explain: Access-Control-Max-Age only controls how long the result of the preflight (the allowed methods and headers) may be cached, subject to each browser's own maximum. It does not affect caching of the real response or any cookie.

blocks.question: A cross-origin fetch fails. Why can't the page's JavaScript find out whether the cause was a missing ACAO header or a server error?
options: Because the server never received the request
Because fetch() does not support error handling
Because the Origin header was stripped
CORS failures are deliberately reported to script only as a generic error; details go to the developer console
blocks.explain: If scripts learned the exact reason, a page could probe other origins and learn about them. So the script only sees a TypeError, while the developer console shows the detailed reason for whoever is debugging.

lessons.title: CORS with credentials, and the misconfigurations that leak data

blocks.md:
By default a cross-origin `fetch()` sends **no cookies**. To send them the page must ask, with `credentials: "include"` (or `withCredentials = true` on the older XMLHttpRequest API). The browser then releases the response only if the server answers with **both**:

- `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, and
- `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` set to the **exact** requesting origin. The wildcard `*` is not allowed with credentials, and the browser blocks the response if it sees one.

This pairing is where the danger is. A credentialed response is personal data, fetched with the victim's own session.

blocks.code:
GET /api/me HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Origin: https://app.example.com
Cookie: __Host-sid=7f3a9c41e2b8

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
Vary: Origin
Content-Type: application/json

{"email": "ana@example.com", "apiKey": "k_51c..."}
blocks.caption: Correct when app.example.com is genuinely trusted. Every origin you echo here can read this user's data with their cookie.

blocks.md:
Maintaining a list of trusted origins is effort, so code takes shortcuts. PortSwigger's Web Security Academy (free training from the makers of Burp Suite, a widely used web testing proxy) lists the common ones:

1. **Reflecting any origin**: copying the request's `Origin` into ACAO with credentials allowed. Any website can then read the user's data.
2. **Broken matching**: checking that the origin *ends with* `example.com` (so `https://hackersexample.com` passes) or *starts with* `https://example.com` (so `https://example.com.evil-user.net` passes).
3. **Trusting `null`**: browsers send `Origin: null` from sandboxed iframes, `data:` and `file:` documents and some redirects, and an attacker can produce those on purpose.
4. **Trusting an `http://` subdomain**: a network attacker can inject script into that plain-HTTP origin and read the HTTPS API through it.
5. **Trusting a subdomain with XSS**: the trust extends to whoever can run script there.

blocks.title: Why string matching on origins fails

scenes.caption: A genuine origin. The suffix check passes as intended.
Anyone can register hackersexample.com. Its origin also ends with example.com, so the suffix check grants it access.
The prefix check fails in the other direction: example.com.evil-user.net is an ordinary subdomain of evil-user.net that starts with the trusted string.
Exact comparison against a fixed set: both attacker origins are rejected and the genuine one passes. No parsing, no regex.

blocks.caption: Express (a Node.js web framework) middleware. The fix never echoes an origin it has not matched exactly, and never trusts null.

blocks.md:
**Why the fix works.** The browser releases a credentialed response only to the origin named in ACAO. If that name comes from a fixed list of origins you control, served over HTTPS and free of XSS, only those pages can read the data. The `Vary: Origin` line stops a cache from serving one origin's permissive answer to another.

PortSwigger adds two more points. Internal sites often answer `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` without credentials, assuming the network keeps outsiders away; but a public page opened by an employee can use that browser to read them, so avoid wildcards on intranets. And remember the previous lesson's warning: CORS says who may *read*, so the server must still check that this user may see this data.

**Defender view.** *Prevent*: one central, exact allowlist; no `null`; no wildcards on internal services; `SameSite=Lax` on session cookies also keeps them off cross-site `fetch()` calls, which takes much of the sting out of a CORS mistake. *Detect*: probe your own APIs by sending requests with made-up `Origin` values (scanners such as Burp Suite do this automatically) and alert if any response reflects them with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. In access logs, credentialed API requests whose `Origin` is not one of your own front ends deserve a look. *Respond*: fix the policy, then rotate any secrets (API keys, tokens) those endpoints returned.

blocks.question: A browser makes a cross-origin `fetch` with `credentials: "include"`. The response has `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. What happens?
options: The browser blocks the script from reading the response
The script reads the response, since * allows everyone
The browser retries without cookies
The server is forced to resend with the exact origin
blocks.explain: With credentials, the wildcard is not acceptable: the server must name the exact origin. The browser sees * and withholds the response, reporting a CORS error in the console. This rule exists to stop accidental exposure of personal data to every site.

blocks.question: An API trusts any origin that fully matches the regular expression `https://.*example\.com`. Which origin would it wrongly trust?
options: https://app.example.com
https://example.com
https://hackersexample.com
http://app.example.com
blocks.explain: The .* before example.com matches any characters, including none and including no dot, so hackersexample.com matches. The http origin fails because the pattern requires https. Exact comparison against a list avoids both mistakes.

blocks.question: Why is trusting `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: null` dangerous?
options: null is the origin of every localhost page
Attackers can make a browser send Origin: null, for example from a sandboxed iframe or a data: URL
null disables the same-origin policy entirely
It is not dangerous; null means no origin can read
blocks.explain: Browsers send Origin: null from several unusual contexts, and an attacker controls some of them, such as a sandboxed iframe on their own page. Trusting null therefore trusts the attacker. PortSwigger recommends never allowlisting it.

lessons.title: Content Security Policy: telling the browser which scripts to trust

blocks.md:
Lesson 1 showed that any script in your page runs with your origin's full power. **Cross-site scripting** (XSS) is the bug where attacker-supplied text, such as a comment, a name or a URL parameter, ends up in your page in a form the browser runs as code. The name was [settled on by a small group of Microsoft security engineers](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/archive/blogs/dross/happy-10th-birthday-cross-site-scripting) in January 2000, and the usual abbreviation is XSS. The real fix is to encode or sanitize data where it enters the page, covered in the client-side attacks course.

**Content Security Policy** (CSP) is the second layer: a response header in which the site tells the browser which scripts and other resources the page is allowed to load and run. If an injection slips through, the browser refuses to run code the policy did not approve.

A policy is a list of **directives** separated by semicolons. **Fetch directives** say where each kind of resource may come from: `script-src` for JavaScript, `style-src` for CSS, `img-src` for images, `connect-src` for `fetch()` targets, and `default-src` as the fallback for any fetch directive not listed. Values include:

- `'self'`: the page's own origin. `'none'`: nothing.
- Hosts or schemes such as `https://cdn.example.net` or `https:`.
- `'nonce-R4nd0m'`: allow only `<script>` elements carrying `nonce="R4nd0m"`. A **nonce** is a value used only once (MDN glosses it as "number used once", though the word is older English, from "for the nonce", meaning for this one occasion): random and fresh for every response, so an attacker cannot know it in advance.
- `'sha256-...'`: allow only a script whose content has exactly this hash.

Once `script-src` or `default-src` is set, inline `<script>` blocks, inline event handlers such as `onerror="..."`, `javascript:` URLs and `eval()` are all blocked unless you explicitly allow them.

blocks.caption: object-src 'none' blocks plugin content; base-uri 'none' stops an injected <base> tag from redirecting relative script URLs. report-to sends violations to your endpoint.

blocks.title: The browser's decision for each script under a nonce policy

scenes.caption: The server's own script tag carries nonce=R4nd0mV4lue, matching the header for this response. It runs.
An attacker's comment injected an inline script. It has no nonce (they could not know this response's value), so it is blocked and reported.
An injected img tag with an onerror handler. Inline event handlers are blocked under any script-src without 'unsafe-inline'.
An injected script tag pointing at an attacker's server. No nonce, so blocked, whatever the host.
app.js (trusted by nonce) creates a new script element. With 'strict-dynamic', trust passes to scripts that trusted scripts load, so it runs. Without it, it would be blocked.

labels.tag:
script added by
app.js at runtime

blocks.caption: Nonces need a server that renders each response. For static pages, use script hashes instead, which do not change between responses.

blocks.md:
Why not just list allowed hosts? MDN explains that **allowlist policies** are hard to get right: they often include domains that host files an attacker can abuse, and they grow huge (MDN cites a case where integrating Google Analytics asked for 187 Google domains). A **strict** policy based on nonces or hashes does not care where a script is hosted, only whether the server vouched for it in this response.

Also note: if a directive contains a nonce or hash, browsers ignore `'unsafe-inline'` in it. [web.dev's strict CSP guide](https://web.dev/articles/strict-csp) uses this to stay compatible with very old browsers: they fall back to `'unsafe-inline'`, modern ones ignore it.

**Real cases.** The Samy worm (lesson 3) ran its code through a `javascript:` URL hidden inside CSS, which some browsers of 2005 executed, and assembled blocked words such as `innerHTML` with `eval()`. Both are things a modern CSP refuses by default. The British Airways breach of 2018 is a harder test, covered in lesson 12: attackers modified a script BA itself served, so a policy that trusted the site's own files would have run it. Directives such as `connect-src`, which limits where scripts may send data, plus violation reports, give defenders a chance to notice data heading somewhere new.

**Deploying and detecting.** Roll out with `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only`: the browser enforces nothing but reports every violation, so you can fix your own inline scripts first. When both headers are present, the enforced policy is applied and the report-only one only reports. Violations arrive as JSON (type `csp-violation`) at the endpoint named in `Reporting-Endpoints`. In production, a burst of reports with the same blocked URL or the same injected inline code across many users is a strong sign that someone found an injection point.

CSP is defence in depth, not a fix. A permissive policy with `'unsafe-inline'` stops almost nothing, and even a strict policy cannot help if your own trusted script takes attacker text and passes it to `eval()` or builds script elements from it. Encode output and validate input first; then add CSP.

blocks.question: A page sends `Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'nonce-abc123' 'unsafe-inline'`. An attacker injects `<script>steal()</script>` with no nonce. What happens?
options: It runs, because 'unsafe-inline' allows inline scripts
It runs only in report-only mode
The whole policy is invalid and ignored
It is blocked, because 'unsafe-inline' is ignored when the directive contains a nonce
blocks.explain: When a nonce or hash is present in the directive, supporting browsers ignore 'unsafe-inline'. The injected script lacks the nonce, so it is blocked. Old browsers that do not understand nonces fall back to 'unsafe-inline', which is why sites sometimes list both.

blocks.question: Why must a CSP nonce be different on every response?
options: A fixed nonce can be learned once and then copied into injected script tags, defeating the policy
Browsers cache nonces and refuse repeats
Nonces expire after 60 seconds
HTTP/2 requires unique header values
blocks.explain: The nonce works only because the attacker cannot predict it. If it is the same on every response, an attacker reads it from any page view and adds nonce="..." to their injected tag, which the browser will then run.

lessons.title: Frames and clickjacking: X-Frame-Options and frame-ancestors

blocks.md:
An **iframe** (inline frame) is an element that shows a whole other page inside the current one, as a nested browsing context. Maps, video players and payment forms are usually iframes. When the framed page is cross-origin, SOP stops the parent from reading or changing its DOM, and the framed page keeps its own origin, cookies and scripts.

But the parent still controls *where* the frame sits and *how it looks*: its size, its position, and its opacity, including fully invisible.

**Clickjacking** (a blend of *click* and *hijacking*, coined in 2008 by security researchers Jeremiah Grossman and Robert Hansen) uses exactly that. PortSwigger defines it as an interface-based attack where a user is tricked into clicking actionable content on a hidden website by clicking some other content on a decoy website. The attacker's page shows "Claim your prize", and directly over the button, in an invisible iframe, sits your bank's "Confirm transfer" button. The click lands on the bank's page, in the user's logged-in session.

Anti-forgery tokens do not help: the click happens on the real bank page, which includes its own valid token. The defence has to come from the framed site saying who may frame it.

blocks.title: How a hidden frame steals a click

scenes.caption: The user sees an ordinary page with a button and decides to click it.
The page also loads bank.example in an iframe. If the user is logged in and the session cookie is sent to framed loads, it shows their real account.
CSS makes the iframe fully transparent and places the bank's button exactly over the prize button. Shown side by side here for clarity.
The click goes to the topmost element: the bank's button. The bank receives a genuine request with a valid token from its own page.
With frame-ancestors 'none' on the bank's response, the browser refuses to render it in the frame. The overlay is empty and the click hits only the decoy.

blocks.md:
Two response headers let a page refuse to be framed:

- **`X-Frame-Options`** (XFO, the older header). `DENY` means never in any frame; `SAMEORIGIN` means only when **every** ancestor frame has the page's own origin. The old `ALLOW-FROM` value is obsolete, and modern browsers that see it ignore the whole header, leaving the page frameable.
- **CSP `frame-ancestors`** (the modern, more flexible replacement). `'none'` means never; `'self'` and a list of origins or schemes allow those parents. Each ancestor in a chain of nested frames is checked.

Both work **only as HTTP headers**. Put in a `<meta>` tag, XFO has no effect and `frame-ancestors` is not supported. Also, `frame-ancestors` does **not** fall back to `default-src`: a policy of `default-src 'none'` alone still lets anyone frame the page.

blocks.code:
# Vulnerable: no framing headers at all, so any site may frame the page.
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'

# Vulnerable: obsolete value; modern browsers ignore the whole header.
X-Frame-Options: ALLOW-FROM https://partner.example

# Fixed: nobody may frame it (XFO kept for very old browsers).
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'
X-Frame-Options: DENY

# Fixed, when one partner must embed you:
Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self' https://partner.example
blocks.caption: The first response looks locked down but sets no framing rule, because frame-ancestors has no default-src fallback.

scenes.caption: The user opens the decoy page. Its HTML contains an iframe pointing at bank.example/transfer.
The browser requests the framed page. Under SameSite=Lax or Strict the session cookie is not sent on this cross-site iframe load, so the page would show logged out anyway.
The bank answers with frame-ancestors 'none'. The browser checks the parent's origin against it and renders nothing in the frame.

blocks.md: **Defender view.** *Prevent*: send `frame-ancestors 'none'` (or a tight list) on every HTML response, especially pages that change state, plus `X-Frame-Options: DENY` for old browsers; keep session cookies `SameSite=Lax` or `Strict` so framed pages load logged out. *Detect*: CSP violation reports include framing refusals, which show who is trying to frame you; a quick check is loading your page inside an iframe on a test page you own. *Respond*: add the header at the web server or CDN layer so no route is missed, then review state-changing actions that were reachable in one click.

blocks.question: A page sends only `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'`. Can an attacker's site frame it?
options: No, 'none' blocks everything including framing
Only if the attacker's site is same-site
Yes, because frame-ancestors does not fall back to default-src
No, because browsers block framing by default
blocks.explain: frame-ancestors is a navigation directive with no default-src fallback. Without frame-ancestors or X-Frame-Options, any site may embed the page, which is also the browser default.

blocks.question: A developer adds `<meta http-equiv="X-Frame-Options" content="deny">` to the page HTML. Is the page now protected from clickjacking?
options: Yes, meta tags are equivalent to headers
No; X-Frame-Options is only honoured as an HTTP response header
Yes, but only in Chrome
No, because DENY must be uppercase
blocks.explain: MDN states that setting X-Frame-Options in a meta element has no effect. The same goes for frame-ancestors, which is not supported in meta. Both must be sent as real response headers.

lessons.title: postMessage: talking across origins on purpose, and safely

blocks.md:
Sometimes two origins *want* to talk. A shop at `https://shop.example` embeds a payment form from `https://pay.example` in an iframe, and needs to know when payment finished. SOP forbids each from touching the other's DOM. `window.postMessage()` is the sanctioned channel: one window sends a message to another window it has a reference to (an iframe's `contentWindow`, a popup from `window.open()`, or `window.opener` / `window.parent`).

- **Sending**: `otherWindow.postMessage(message, targetOrigin)`. The message is copied with the *structured clone* algorithm, so objects can be sent without converting them to strings. `targetOrigin` names the origin the receiving window must have, or the message is not delivered.
- **Receiving**: listen for the `message` event. `event.data` is the message, `event.origin` is the sender's origin at the time it sent, and `event.source` is the sender's window, for replies.

blocks.title: Messages between a shop, its payment frame and an intruder

scenes.caption: The shop sends the order to its payment iframe, naming https://pay.example as targetOrigin. If the frame had been navigated elsewhere, the message would not be delivered.
The payment frame replies to the parent, again naming the exact target origin.
evil.example opened the shop in a popup, so it holds a window reference. Any window with a reference can post a message to it.
A listener that checks event.origin sees https://evil.example and ignores the message. A listener that does not check marks order 42 as paid.
Sending with targetOrigin '*' is the mirror bug: if the frame was navigated to an attacker's page, the secret is delivered to it.

blocks.caption: The vulnerable receiver accepts messages from anyone and writes their text into the page as HTML, which turns a stray message into XSS.

blocks.md:
**Why the fix works.** `event.origin` is filled in by the browser, not the sender, so a page cannot fake it. Comparing it with `!==` against one exact origin rejects everyone else. Validating the shape of `event.data` protects you if the trusted sender itself is ever compromised. Writing with `textContent` instead of `innerHTML` means the text is shown, never parsed as HTML. And because a message is only a claim, the shop confirms the payment with its own server rather than trusting `paid: true`.

On the sending side, an exact `targetOrigin` means that if the frame or popup was navigated to another origin without your knowledge, the browser drops the message instead of handing it over. MDN's advice for receivers is even simpler: if you do not expect messages from other sites, do not add a `message` listener at all.

blocks.title: The fixed listener handling three messages

scenes.caption: A message from the real payment frame. The origin matches exactly.
The shape is valid, so the shop asks its own server whether order 42 is paid, rather than believing the message.
A message from the attacker's tab. The browser set event.origin, so it cannot be forged. The listener returns at line 2.
A look-alike origin. An indexOf or startsWith check would accept it; the exact comparison does not.

blocks.md: **Defender view.** *Prevent*: search your code and third-party widgets for `addEventListener("message"` and for `postMessage(` with `"*"`; every listener needs an exact origin check and input validation, and should never pass message data to `innerHTML`, `eval()` or a URL used for navigation. *Detect*: these bugs live entirely in the browser, so server logs see little; code review, static analysis rules for message listeners and CSP violation reports (if a message triggers blocked script) are your signals. *Respond*: fix the listener and treat any data it could have changed (orders, settings) as untrusted until checked on the server.

blocks.question: A widget's listener checks `if (event.origin.indexOf("pay.example") !== -1)`. Which sender can get past it?
options: Only https://pay.example
No one, because event.origin cannot be faked
Only same-origin pages
https://pay.example.attacker.net
blocks.explain: event.origin really is set by the browser, but the check only asks whether the string contains pay.example anywhere. An attacker who controls pay.example.attacker.net passes it. Compare the whole origin exactly.

blocks.question: Why is `popup.postMessage(secret, "*")` risky even though you opened the popup yourself?
options: The popup may have been navigated to another origin, and * delivers the message to whatever origin it now has
Because * encrypts the message with a weak key
Because * sends the message to every open tab
It is not risky if the popup was opened by your own code
blocks.explain: MDN warns that a malicious site can change a window's location without your knowledge. With a specific targetOrigin, the browser drops the message if the window is no longer on that origin; with * it delivers the secret to whoever is there now.

lessons.title: HTTPS, mixed content and HSTS: keeping the network out

blocks.md:
Every rule so far assumed the bytes arriving from `https://bank.example` really came from the bank. On plain HTTP that is false: anyone on the path (the café Wi-Fi, a compromised router) can read and rewrite traffic. MDN calls this a **manipulator in the middle** (MitM) attack. **HTTPS** is HTTP sent over **TLS** (Transport Layer Security, the successor of SSL, Secure Sockets Layer), which encrypts the traffic and checks the server's certificate, so a MitM can neither read nor silently change it.

Origins include the scheme for exactly this reason: `http://bank.example` and `https://bank.example` are different origins, and the http one must be assumed attacker-controlled on a hostile network.

**Mixed content** is an HTTPS page that loads subresources over HTTP. Those resources can be read or modified in transit, and a modified script controls the whole page. Browsers now handle it in two classes: - **Upgradable**: ``, `

blocks.code: # Header that upgrades every insecure subresource URL on the page, # useful while old content still contains http:// links: Content-Security-Policy: upgrade-insecure-requests
blocks.caption: The developer console warns for each upgraded or blocked request. upgrade-insecure-requests does not upgrade links to other origins, so it is not a substitute for HSTS.

blocks.title: HSTS in action: learn once, refuse plain HTTP later

scenes.caption: First visit, at home. The user follows an old http:// link to example.com. The browser has no HSTS entry for it, so this first request is plain HTTP.
The server redirects permanently to HTTPS. The redirect itself must not carry the HSTS header, because browsers ignore it over HTTP.
Over HTTPS the response carries the HSTS header. The browser records example.com and its subdomains as HTTPS-only for a year.
Weeks later, at an airport, the user joins a rogue access point and opens http://login.example.com. The browser upgrades it to https before any byte leaves.
The attacker answers with a fake certificate. Because the host is HSTS, the error page has no Continue button. The password is never typed into the fake site.

blocks.md:
HSTS still trusts the first visit. The **HSTS preload list**, run by Google at hstspreload.org and used by all major browsers, removes that by shipping your domain name inside the browser. Requirements include a valid certificate, HTTPS on every subdomain, and a header with `max-age` of at least 31536000, `includeSubDomains` and `preload`. Be careful: hstspreload.org itself now says HSTS is recommended but preloading is not, because many browsers already upgrade navigations to HTTPS and removal from the list is slow and painful.

Other details from MDN: HSTS identifies a host by name only (an IP address cannot be an HSTS host) and applies to all its ports. Each new header pushes the expiry forward. Sending `max-age=0` over HTTPS turns HSTS off.

blocks.code:
# hstspreload.org's suggested ramp-up (first three stages): increase max-age
# in stages, watching for broken subdomains, waiting a full max-age each time.
# The last line is the long-term value from its example header.
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=300; includeSubDomains       # 5 minutes
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=604800; includeSubDomains    # 1 week
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=2592000; includeSubDomains   # 1 month
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains  # 2 years
blocks.caption: Ramp slowly: once a browser has stored a long max-age, a subdomain that cannot do HTTPS becomes unreachable for those users.

blocks.md: Firesheep's full fix is three layers: **HTTPS on every page** (nothing worth stealing in clear text), **`Secure` cookies** (the session never rides a plain request, even one an attacker tricks the browser into making), and **HSTS** (the browser refuses plain HTTP and certificate click-through for the whole site).

**Defender view.** *Prevent*: serve everything over HTTPS, redirect port 80 with a 301, send HSTS on every HTTPS response (including each subdomain, since a browser may visit a subdomain first), fix mixed content rather than relying on upgrades. *Detect*: browser console warnings and CSP reports list mixed content; external scanners show which hosts lack HSTS; certificate errors reported by users on a network are a MitM signal. *Respond*: an expired or broken certificate on an HSTS host locks users out completely, so treat certificate renewal as a monitored, alerting job.

blocks.question: A site sends `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000` in a response served over plain HTTP. What does the browser do?
options: Stores the host as HSTS for a year
Stores it but only for the current session
Ignores the header, because HSTS is only accepted over HTTPS
Upgrades this one response to HTTPS
blocks.explain: Browsers ignore HSTS sent over HTTP. Otherwise a MitM could inject a header for a site that does not support HTTPS (locking users out) or strip and replace it. The header must arrive over a secure connection to count.

blocks.question: An HTTPS page contains `` and ``. What do current browsers do?
options: Load both over HTTP and show a warning
Upgrade the image to HTTPS and block the script
Block both
Block the image and upgrade the script
blocks.explain: Images loaded via src are upgradable content: the browser tries the https URL instead. Scripts are blockable content, because a modified script would control the page, so the insecure request is not made at all.

lessons.title: Subresource Integrity and the trust you hand to third-party scripts

blocks.md:
Lesson 1 ended with a warning: a `<script src>` from someone else's server runs with your origin's power, and you trust whoever controls that server, today and in the future. Many sites load libraries from a **CDN** (content delivery network: a set of servers in many locations that serve copies of files from near the user). If the CDN or the file is compromised, so is every page that includes it. This is a **supply chain attack**.

**Subresource Integrity** (SRI) lets the page pin the exact file it expects. You add an `integrity` attribute holding a cryptographic hash of the file: a short fingerprint computed from its bytes with an algorithm such as SHA-384 (SHA is Secure Hash Algorithm, 384 the output size in bits), where any change to the file gives a completely different value. The browser hashes what actually arrived and refuses to run it unless the hashes match.

blocks.code:
# Compute the SRI value for a file you have reviewed:
openssl dgst -sha384 -binary lib.js | openssl base64 -A
# For a lib.js containing exactly:  console.log("hi");  plus a newline
# tdnWtBkj5+038HkeFOzlN0GdBuwDpXaWFs1Dhs560d67HmXunuEg4R3e+iEGk0Ho

<script
  src="https://cdn.example.net/lib.js"
  integrity="sha384-tdnWtBkj5+038HkeFOzlN0GdBuwDpXaWFs1Dhs560d67HmXunuEg4R3e+iEGk0Ho"
  crossorigin="anonymous"></script>
blocks.caption: Allowed algorithms are sha256, sha384 and sha512. The value is the algorithm name, a dash, and the base64 digest.

blocks.md:
How the browser checks, per MDN:

1. It fetches the file **with CORS**. That is why `crossorigin="anonymous"` is required and why the CDN must send `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` (usually `*`). A plain script tag uses *no-cors* mode, where the page can use a response but not read it, and browsers refuse integrity checks in no-cors mode: otherwise a page could probe other sites' private files by guessing hashes and watching which loads succeed.
2. If the attribute lists several hashes, it uses only those made with the **strongest** algorithm present (SHA-512 over SHA-384 over SHA-256) and accepts the file if any of them match.
3. On a mismatch it does not run the file and reports a network error.

blocks.title: The SRI check, with the real hashes of two tiny files

scenes.caption: The CDN returns the reviewed file, console.log("hi"); with a newline. Its SHA-384 starts tdnWtBkj, matching the attribute, so it runs.
Someone changes one character on the CDN: console.log("hi!");. The digest becomes GiiObSaY..., nothing like the old one. The browser refuses to execute it.
The CDN stops sending Access-Control-Allow-Origin. A CORS-mode fetch fails before any hashing, so integrity checks also fail closed.

blocks.md:
**Real case: polyfill.io (2024).** A *polyfill* is code that adds modern browser features to older browsers (Remy Sharp, a web developer, named it after Polyfilla, a filler paste for cracks in walls). Over 100,000 sites loaded one from `cdn.polyfill.io`. According to Sansec, a security firm that investigated, a company bought the domain and the project's GitHub account in February 2024, and when Sansec reported in June 2024 the CDN had been caught injecting malware into pages on mobile devices, redirecting some visitors to a sports betting site via a fake Google Analytics domain. The code avoided admins and ran only on certain devices at certain hours, which made it hard to spot.

SRI was of little use here: Sansec notes the polyfill file was generated dynamically from the request's headers, so there was no single file whose hash a page could pin. The fixes were to remove it (the original author said modern browsers no longer need it) or switch to trustworthy mirrors that Cloudflare and Fastly put up, and Cloudflare also rewrote references at its edge.

**Real case: British Airways (2018).** Attackers modified a JavaScript file served by BA's own website so that card details customers typed on the payment page were also sent to an attacker-run domain, `baways.com`. RiskIQ, a security firm, traced it to a tampered copy of the Modernizr library and attributed it to Magecart, a name for card-skimming crews active since 2015, as [The Register reported](https://www.theregister.com/security/2018/09/11/british-airways-hack-infosec-experts-finger-third-party-scripts-on-payment-pages/442752). The UK Information Commissioner's Office later fined BA GBP 20 million for the breach, which affected more than 400,000 customers ([BBC](https://www.bbc.com/news/technology-54568784)).

Here the file was first-party and the attackers had access to BA's systems, so they could have changed an `integrity` attribute too. SRI protects you from **someone else's** server; for your own, you need change monitoring on what you serve.

SRI only works for files that never change between requests. It cannot pin a script that is generated per request or a library loaded as "latest". Pin exact versions, self-host what you can, and keep the list of third-party scripts on sensitive pages (login, payment) as short as possible.

**Defender view.** *Prevent*: SRI on every third-party script and stylesheet; self-host where practical; a strict CSP so a new script source cannot appear silently. An `Integrity-Policy` header (in Chrome, Firefox and Safari for scripts; stylesheet support is still experimental) blocks scripts that lack integrity metadata, with an `Integrity-Policy-Report-Only` version for a trial run. *Detect*: CSP and integrity violation reports; monitoring that fetches your payment pages from outside and alerts when any script's content or any outbound data destination changes (this is how researchers reconstructed the BA timeline from scans over time). *Respond*: remove the script, rotate anything it could read, and notify affected users and regulators as the law requires.

blocks.question: A script tag has `integrity="sha256-AAA... sha384-BBB..."`. The file's SHA-256 matches AAA but its SHA-384 does not match BBB. What does the browser do?
options: Runs it, because one hash matched
Runs it with a console warning
Asks the user
Refuses it: only the strongest algorithm listed (SHA-384) is checked, and it does not match
blocks.explain: MDN: the browser selects the hashes made with the strongest function present and ignores weaker ones. Only sha384-BBB is compared, it fails, and the script is not executed.

blocks.question: Why does an SRI-protected cross-origin script need `crossorigin="anonymous"` and an `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header?
options: Integrity checks are only allowed on CORS fetches; in no-cors mode they would let pages probe the content of other sites' private files
To encrypt the file in transit
To send the user's cookies to the CDN
Because SHA-384 requires a CORS header
blocks.explain: If integrity worked in no-cors mode, an attacker's page could request a private resource with a guessed hash and learn from success or failure whether the guess was right. Requiring CORS means the server has agreed the content may be read anyway.

lessons.title: Site isolation: separate processes as a second wall

blocks.md:
SOP is enforced by checks inside the browser's own code, and that code has bugs. Chrome splits the browser into a **browser process** (the trusted part that handles the network, cookies, files and the window) and **renderer processes** (the part that parses HTML and runs a page's JavaScript). Renderers run in a **sandbox**, an operating-system jail that stops them touching files and devices directly.

Historically one renderer could hold pages from many sites, for example a news page and the ad iframe inside it. If anything let one page read memory belonging to another in the same process, SOP's checks were bypassed.

The Chromium project names three threats that do exactly that:

1. **A compromised renderer**: a memory bug in the renderer lets attacker script run arbitrary code inside that process. Chromium counted between 5 and 15 such potentially exploitable renderer bugs per release in releases M69 to M73 (Chrome milestones 69 to 73, from 2018 and 2019).
2. **UXSS** (universal cross-site scripting): a browser bug, not a site bug, that lets a page bypass SOP and run script in other sites' pages.
3. **Side channels such as Spectre** (named after its root cause, speculative execution): a 2018 class of CPU flaw in which *speculative execution* (the processor running instructions ahead of time in case they are needed) leaves traces that let code infer memory it should not read. Script could read any memory in its own process, with no browser bug at all.

blocks.title: From shared renderers to one process per site

scenes.caption: Before isolation: the news page and its cross-site ad iframe can share one renderer process. SOP checks inside that process keep them apart.
A malicious ad uses a Spectre-style side channel or a renderer bug. Everything in the same process, including the news page's data, is now readable. SOP checks are simply bypassed.
With Site Isolation, cross-site documents always get different processes, even an iframe inside a page (an out-of-process iframe). The ad lives alone in its own renderer.

The ad's renderer asks for bank.example JSON. Cross-site HTML, XML, JSON and PDF are not delivered into its process unless the server allows it via CORS, so even a full process compromise cannot read them.
The browser process also checks what each renderer asks for, and on desktop it can terminate a renderer that requests another site's data.

blocks.md:
Chrome turned **Site Isolation** on for all sites on desktop in Chrome 67 (2018), in response to Spectre. From Chrome 77 it also defends against fully compromised renderers and UXSS on desktop. On Android, where memory is tighter, it covers sites users log in to on devices with at least 2 GB of RAM. Firefox's equivalent, Project Fission, shipped to desktop Firefox in version 95.

Note the unit: **site**, not origin. Chromium explains it uses sites to stay compatible with pages that set `document.domain` to talk across subdomains. So `login.example.com` and `blog.example.com` may share a process, one more reason a weak subdomain is a risk to the whole site.

blocks.caption: COOP (Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy) and COEP (Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy). Browsers make SharedArrayBuffer (memory shared between threads) available only when both headers are set.

blocks.md: Site isolation is **defence in depth** for the browser itself. It does not change what web pages are allowed to do, so it will not stop XSS, CSRF or a bad CORS policy. It limits the damage when the browser's own enforcement fails.

**Defender view.** For most teams the job is small but real: keep browsers updated (renderer bugs are patched constantly, and enterprise policies should not disable site isolation), serve sensitive data with correct `Content-Type` headers and without permissive CORS so the browser knows to keep it out of other sites' processes, and use COOP on sensitive pages so attacker-opened windows cannot share their browsing context. Renderer processes being terminated for security violations, visible in browser crash reporting, can be a sign of probing.

blocks.question: Why does Chrome's Site Isolation put processes per site rather than per origin?
options: Origins are too hard to compute
Because cookies are scoped per site
To stay compatible with pages that use document.domain to communicate across subdomains of one site
Per-origin processes are impossible on Windows
blocks.explain: Chromium's documentation says it uses sites instead of origins to avoid breaking existing pages that change document.domain to talk across subdomains. The cost is that same-site subdomains may share a process.

blocks.question: Which threat does Site Isolation address that the same-origin policy alone cannot?
options: A stored XSS bug in your own site
A malicious page reading another site's data from shared process memory via Spectre
A CSRF attack using a hidden form
A session cookie sent over HTTP
blocks.explain: Spectre lets script read memory in its own process without any software bug, so SOP checks never get a chance to refuse. Putting each site in its own process means that memory simply is not there to read. XSS, CSRF and cookie leaks are web-level bugs that site isolation does not change.

lessons.title: The map: which bug class gets around which rule

blocks.md:
You now have every piece of the model. Pages from different **origins** share one browser; the **same-origin policy** stops them reading each other; **cookies** carry identity and their attributes limit where it travels; **CORS** is the server's deliberate exception for reads; **CSP**, **SRI** and **framing headers** let a site restrict what runs in or around its pages; **HTTPS** and **HSTS** keep the network out; **site isolation** backs up the browser's own enforcement.

Every web bug class in the courses that follow is a way around one of these rules. Knowing *which* rule a bug defeats tells you which defence actually works against it.

blocks.title: Which control defends against which bug class (2 main, 1 helps)

scenes.caption: Rows are attacks, columns are the rules from this course. Notice the SOP column is almost empty: every attack here works by going around it, not through it.
XSS runs inside your origin, so SOP does not apply. CSP is the browser-side backstop; HttpOnly only stops cookie theft. The real fix is output encoding (next courses).
CSRF abuses allowed cross-origin writes plus automatic cookies. SameSite is the main browser control; preflights protect JSON APIs. Anti-forgery tokens complete it.
Clickjacking abuses allowed embedding. frame-ancestors and X-Frame-Options stop it; SameSite makes framed pages load logged out.
CORS misconfiguration is the server switching SOP off for the wrong origins. The fix is in the CORS rules; SameSite keeps session cookies off cross-site fetches.
Session hijacking on the network (Firesheep) is beaten by HTTPS everywhere, HSTS and the Secure attribute.
Malicious third-party script (polyfill.io, Magecart) is trusted code by design. SRI pins static files; CSP limits sources and destinations; monitoring catches the rest.
postMessage bugs are pure code mistakes: no header fixes them. Only exact origin checks and validation do, with CSP softening any XSS that results.
When the browser itself fails (renderer bugs, UXSS, Spectre), site isolation is the layer that still holds.

blocks.md:
Where each class is taught in depth, with the vulnerable code next to the fix:

- **XSS** (reflected, stored, DOM-based), **CSRF** and **clickjacking**: the client-side attacks course, with the Samy worm (2005) and the British Airways Magecart skimmer (2018) as worked cases.
- **Injection** (SQL, command, template): the injection course. These are server bugs, but a stored injection often ends as XSS in someone's browser.
- **Broken access control**: the access control course. Remember the warning from the CORS lessons: browser rules decide who may *read* a response in a browser; only the server decides who may *have* the data.
- **Supply chain**: the supply chain security course, which picks up polyfill.io-style takeovers and dependency risk.

blocks.code:
# A response-header baseline for an HTML page that shows user data.
# Each line maps to a lesson in this course.
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains        # L11
Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'nonce-R4nd0mV4lue' 'strict-dynamic';
  object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none';
  report-to csp-endpoint                                               # L8, L9
Reporting-Endpoints: csp-endpoint="https://example.com/csp-reports"
X-Frame-Options: DENY                                                  # L9
Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin                                # L13
Set-Cookie: __Host-sid=7f3a9c41e2b8; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Path=/   # L4, L5
# No Access-Control-Allow-* headers unless a known origin must read it  # L6, L7
blocks.caption: A starting point, not a complete defence: none of these headers fixes an injection bug or a missing authorization check on the server.

blocks.md: Ask two questions of every web bug: **whose origin is the attacker's code running in**, and **which browser rule was supposed to stop it**? If the code runs inside your origin (XSS, malicious third-party script), the browser's cross-origin rules cannot help and you need CSP, SRI and clean output encoding. If it runs in the attacker's origin, the question is which allowance (writes, embedding, CORS, messages) they abused.

**Practise legally.** Only test systems you own or have written permission to test; testing anything else can be a crime under laws such as the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and the UK Computer Misuse Act. Good free, legal places to practise this course's material:

- [PortSwigger Web Security Academy](https://portswigger.net/web-security): free labs on [CORS misconfigurations](https://portswigger.net/web-security/cors), [clickjacking](https://portswigger.net/web-security/clickjacking) and [CSP](https://portswigger.net/web-security/cross-site-scripting/content-security-policy).
- [OWASP Juice Shop](https://owasp.org/www-project-juice-shop/): a deliberately insecure web shop you run locally, from OWASP (the Open Worldwide Application Security Project, a nonprofit).
- Your own browser: open developer tools on any site you use, and read its `Set-Cookie`, CSP, HSTS and CORS headers with this course's checklist.

blocks.question: An attacker finds that a profile page renders bio text as raw HTML, and plants a script there. Which of these defences helps most in the browser?
options: Same-origin policy
Access-Control-Allow-Origin set to the site's own origin
X-Frame-Options: DENY
A strict, nonce-based Content Security Policy
blocks.explain: The planted script runs inside the site's own origin, so SOP and CORS have nothing to say, and framing headers are unrelated. A strict CSP refuses to run script the server did not mark with this response's nonce. The root fix is still encoding the bio on output.

blocks.question: A forum lets users post images. An attacker posts an image URL that points at `https://bank.example/transfer?to=attacker&amount=500`. The bank changes money on a GET. Which rule would have stopped the browser from attaching the user's bank cookie?
options: SameSite=Lax or Strict on the bank's session cookie
Same-origin policy
Subresource Integrity
HSTS
blocks.explain: The image request is cross-origin embedding, which SOP allows, and here it triggers a state change on the server. Under Lax or Strict the cookie is not sent on a cross-site image request, so the bank sees an anonymous request. The deeper bug is changing state on GET, which the CSRF material covers.

blocks.question: Which pairing of bug class and the rule it gets around is correct?
options: Clickjacking gets around CSP script-src
Firesheep got around Site Isolation
CORS misconfiguration is a server telling the browser to relax the same-origin policy for the wrong origin
postMessage bugs are fixed by HSTS
blocks.explain: A CORS misconfiguration is the site itself switching off SOP's read protection for origins it should not trust. Clickjacking abuses embedding (fixed by framing headers), Firesheep abused unencrypted transport (fixed by HTTPS, Secure and HSTS), and postMessage bugs need code fixes.
